cases.claim: The reported charging tour visits four scheduled stops before returning to the depot.
evidence: Evidence states that the charging tour contains four scheduled stops before returning to the depot.

cases.claim: For the tested 80-node instance, the scheduler achieved a lower average response time than FCFS.
evidence: In the evaluated 80-node instance, the proposed scheduler reduced mean response time relative to the FCFS baseline.

cases.claim: The heuristic is not proven to be globally optimal.
evidence: The paper explicitly states that the heuristic does not provide a proof of global optimality.

cases.claim: At a packet-loss rate of 0.05, the stated stability condition is satisfied.
evidence: The stability result holds when packet loss is no greater than 0.08.

cases.claim: Vehicle V2 has enough capacity to carry request R7, considering capacity alone.
evidence: Vehicle V2 has capacity 120 units.
Request R7 requires 40 units.

cases.claim: In that 30-minute simulation setting, ALNS had lower median travel distance than the greedy method.
evidence: Under the same 30-minute simulation horizon, ALNS obtained a smaller median travel distance than the greedy baseline.

cases.claim: A sensor with zero residual energy counts as a dead node under this definition.
evidence: A dead node is defined as a sensor whose residual energy has reached zero.

cases.claim: PSO is used to optimize the charging sequence in the described method.
evidence: The optimization stage uses particle swarm optimization to tune the charging sequence.

cases.claim: All 12 reported instances finished within 300 seconds.
evidence: Across the 12 reported instances, every run completed within the 300-second time limit.

cases.claim: The obstacle-avoidance constraint is derived from the geometric feasibility model in Section 4.
evidence: The article attributes the obstacle-avoidance constraint to the geometric feasibility model introduced in Section 4.

cases.claim: The reported route begins and ends at depot D.
evidence: The charger starts at depot D.
The final route returns to depot D.

cases.claim: The reported experiment succeeded in 93% of its 100 trials.
evidence: The experiment reports a success rate of 0.93 over 100 independent trials.

cases.claim: A schedule that starts service after a node's deadline violates the stated model constraint.
evidence: The model requires every service to begin before the corresponding node deadline.

cases.claim: In the 40-node benchmark, preprocessing removed more than half of the candidate edges.
evidence: For the 40-node benchmark, preprocessing reduced candidate edges from 780 to 214.

cases.claim: The 25 recorded test runs contained zero communication failures.
evidence: No communication failures occurred in any of the 25 recorded test runs.

cases.claim: The evaluated configuration does not include node mobility during a run.
evidence: Method M uses a static node set.
Node positions are fixed throughout each run.

cases.claim: In the reported experiment, the higher tested charger speed was associated with a shorter average tour duration.
evidence: When charger speed increased from 1 m/s to 2 m/s in the reported experiment, average tour duration decreased from 68 to 51 minutes.

cases.claim: High memory use is acknowledged as a limitation of the dynamic programming variant.
evidence: The authors list high memory consumption as a limitation of the dynamic programming variant.

cases.claim: Method A achieved the best objective value among A, B and C on D3.
evidence: On dataset D3, method A ranked first, method B second, and method C third by objective value.

cases.claim: Under the theorem's assumptions, the system has one mobile charger.
evidence: The theorem assumes a single mobile charger and a connected communication graph.

cases.claim: The experiment uses 42 charging targets.
evidence: The experiment uses 24 charging targets.

cases.claim: The method guarantees that every node is serviced before depletion.
evidence: The method does not guarantee that every node is serviced before depletion.

cases.claim: The prototype has already been validated in an outdoor field deployment.
evidence: The prototype was evaluated exclusively in a hardware-in-the-loop simulator and was never deployed outdoors.

cases.claim: The convergence statement is valid for alpha = 0.6.
evidence: The convergence statement is valid only when alpha is in the interval [0, 0.2].

cases.claim: PSO ranked ahead of ALNS on B7.
evidence: On benchmark B7, PSO ranked fourth while ALNS ranked first.

cases.claim: The model contains three mobile chargers.
evidence: The model contains exactly two mobile chargers.

cases.claim: The reported simulation horizon is 2 hours.
evidence: The reported simulation horizon is 90 minutes.

cases.claim: The implementation uses reinforcement learning to choose charging actions.
evidence: The implementation does not use reinforcement learning; decisions are produced by a rule-based scheduler.

cases.claim: The higher penalty coefficient reduced the reported objective value.
evidence: Increasing the penalty coefficient from 1 to 3 increased the reported objective value from 210 to 264.

cases.claim: The evaluated network contains a cycle.
evidence: The evaluated network is a tree with no cycles.

cases.claim: The reported results include experiments on real-world mobility traces.
evidence: All reported results were obtained on synthetic instances; no real-world traces were used.

cases.claim: A request predicted to finish in 22 minutes is accepted under this rule.
evidence: A request is rejected whenever its predicted completion time exceeds 15 minutes.

cases.claim: Vehicle V1 can legally carry a 70-unit request without splitting it.
evidence: Vehicle V1 has a hard payload limit of 50 units.

cases.claim: Algorithm 2 is identified as a genetic algorithm.
evidence: The paper identifies Algorithm 2 as an ALNS procedure.

cases.claim: The table reports an average delay below 10 seconds for method K.
evidence: The table reports an average delay of 18.4 seconds for method K.

cases.claim: The authors released the source code with the paper.
evidence: The appendix states that source code was not released.

cases.claim: The formulation models obstacles that move during optimization.
evidence: The formulation explicitly assumes static obstacles whose locations do not change during optimization.

cases.claim: The optimization objective is to maximize total travel distance.
evidence: The optimization objective is to minimize the number of dead nodes.

cases.claim: The theorem covers disconnected graphs as well.
evidence: The theorem is stated only for connected graphs and explicitly excludes disconnected graphs.

cases.claim: The measured packet delivery ratio exceeds 0.90.
evidence: The measured packet delivery ratio is 0.72.

cases.claim: The strategy reduces energy consumption for every network size and topology.
evidence: The proposed strategy reduced energy consumption on the tested 60-node topology.

cases.claim: Increasing charger density causes longer network lifetime.
evidence: Runs with higher charger density also showed longer network lifetime.

cases.claim: The controller will maintain the same performance after deployment in a real city.
evidence: The controller was evaluated in a simulator using realistic traffic traces.

cases.claim: The heuristic is guaranteed to find the global optimum on every instance.
evidence: The heuristic found the best known solution on 9 of 10 benchmark instances.

cases.claim: Method R has the lowest worst-case delay.
evidence: Method R had the lowest average delay in the reported experiments.

cases.claim: The policy remains stable for arbitrarily long deployments.
evidence: The policy remained stable during a 2-hour evaluation.

cases.claim: Method A reduces travel distance because its neighborhood operator preserves route convexity.
evidence: The paper reports that method A reduces total travel distance.

cases.claim: The new method outperforms PSO on instance X.
evidence: The new method achieved an objective value of 148 on instance X.

cases.claim: The algorithm usually converges in fewer than 100 iterations.
evidence: With random seed 17, the algorithm converged after 84 iterations.

cases.claim: The same method will perform well for mobile wireless chargers.
evidence: The scheduling method performed well for warehouse robots.

cases.claim: The theorem also proves feasibility with three chargers and polygonal obstacles.
evidence: The theorem proves feasibility when there is one charger and no obstacles.

cases.claim: Method A is statistically significantly better than Method B.
evidence: Method A had a mean score of 91.2 and Method B a mean score of 90.8.

cases.claim: The scheduler explicitly prioritizes nodes by residual energy.
evidence: Nodes with lower residual energy were more likely to receive earlier service in the logs.

cases.claim: The system is safe from battery overheating under all operating conditions.
evidence: No battery overheating occurred in 30 laboratory runs.

cases.claim: Performance will continue improving if beta is increased to 1.0.
evidence: Performance improved as beta increased from 0.1 to 0.3 in the reported sweep.

cases.claim: The model does not support obstacles.
evidence: The excerpt describes the routing objective and energy constraint but says nothing about obstacle handling.

cases.claim: Method Z dominates baseline B on every relevant metric and dataset.
evidence: Method Z lowered mean latency in dataset D1.
It used less memory than baseline B in D2.

cases.claim: The optimization problem has a unique global optimum.
evidence: The implementation returned the same solution in five repeated runs.

cases.claim: The prototype is reliable across cities, seasons, and weather conditions.
evidence: The prototype was tested on one university campus for three days.

cases.claim: The authors chose ALNS because it is guaranteed to outperform PSO on this problem class.
evidence: The authors use ALNS in the final solver.
